findings.title: A one-word state "may" live in the state word: two implementations differ on Alloc, and a copy-out loses the function's own changes
findings.why: `[CLO-10]`: "what it captured with a word, in one block of its own made with the value (it carries `Alloc` ...), except that a state of one word or less may be kept in the state word itself, with no block" — "may" leaves the choice to the implementation, and `[EFF-1]`'s `Alloc` ("a function value's state placed on the heap") and so a `@noalloc` verdict follow the choice, against `[PHIL-13]`. `[CLO-10]`: "A call through a list element or a field copies the two words out before the arguments are given and keeps no pointer into the list or field"; `[CLO-18]`: "A call through a stored function value whose functions may change their own state is a change of the place that holds it" — with the state inline in the copied word, the change is made to the copy and nothing says it is written back.
findings.proposed_text: * `[CLO-10]` replace "except that a state of one word or less may be kept in the state word itself, with no block" with: "except that a state of one word or less that the function's body never writes itself (a `copy of` of a `Copy` value it only reads, or an owner or a link it only reads through, no captured name assigned or given another ref in the body) is kept in the state word itself, with no block and no `Alloc`; a state the body may write lives in a block of its own, so that a call through a copy of the two words (a list element, a field, `[BRW-1]`) changes the state the holder keeps. Which of the two a function value has is decided from its captures and its body alone, the same in every implementation (`[PHIL-13]`), and `ember inspect --alloc` reports it." Add to `[CLO-18]`: "The two words copied out before the call (`[CLO-10]`) point at the state the holder keeps, never at a copy of it: a function value that changes its own state has a block, so the change is the holder's after the call."
findings.codes: none new; `E4001` where the state carries `Alloc`

findings.title: `shares p` of a `thread_shared` owner: "a name that is already such an owner" admits a one-thread owner of a block counted for several threads
findings.program:
import std.thread

class Player:
    hp: int = 10

fn look(owns p: thread_shared Player):
    q = shares p                 # <-- [RC-1]: `p` is "a name that is already such an owner"? If accepted, `q` is a `shares Player`: a plain +1 at offset 0, the home count only the making thread may touch
    println(q.hp)

fn main():
    p = thread_shared Player()
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() thread_shared p: look(thread_shared p))
    r = shares p                 # the making thread's plain add to the same word, at the same moment
    h.join()
findings.why: `[RC-1]`: "`shares x`, `shares mut x` and `thread_shared x` are written before a new value, a local of this function that owns its value ... or a name that is already such an owner" — a `thread_shared` name is an owner, and nothing says which words match which; `[OWN-13]`: "`shares x`, one more owner, on this thread, that reads it ... each written only before a new value, a local or an owner"; `[THR-1]` refuses only the reverse (`thread_shared` on a value "made otherwise" is `E7017`). `[RC-4]` point 1: the home count is "read and written only by that thread, with plain instructions"; a `shares` owner made on another thread adds to it with a plain add (`[RT-10]`), a race on the count, and a `shares` type is not `Send`, so nothing else refuses the line.
findings.proposed_text: * `[RC-1]` replace "or a name that is already such an owner" with "or a name that is already an owner of the same kind: `shares x` and `shares mut x` before a `shares` or `shares mut` owner, `thread_shared x` before a `thread_shared` owner. A `shares` or `shares mut` written before a `thread_shared` owner is `E7017`, as `thread_shared` before a `shares` owner is (`[THR-1]`): \"`p` is `thread_shared` (made on line 10), so its owners are counted for several threads; for one more owner write `q = thread_shared p`, and for a name that only reads it `q = ref p`\"." `[OWN-13]`: the same words after "or an owner". `[THR-1]`: add "and the reverse, `shares` or `shares mut` on a `thread_shared` owner, is `E7017` too (`[RC-1]`)". Registry row `E7017`: "an owner word that does not match how the value was made: `thread_shared` on a value not created `thread_shared`, or `shares`/`shares mut` on a `thread_shared` owner".
findings.codes: E7017 (widened: an owner word that does not match how the value was made); shape N15

findings.title: A `defer` registered before a `yield`: nothing says whether it runs when the suspended frame is dropped
findings.program:
import std.fs

gen fn lines_of(path: StrView) -> Generator[String]:
    f = fs.File.open(path).unwrap()
    defer: println("closed")          # registered before the loop
    for line in f.lines():
        yield line.unwrap()

fn main():
    g = lines_of("a.txt")
    first = g.next()                   # suspended inside the `for`; the `defer` is registered
    mem.drop(owns g)                   # <-- [CORO-7]: "drops exactly the locals live at its suspension point"; does "closed" print? Python runs `finally` here
findings.why: `[CORO-7]`: "Dropping a suspended generator drops exactly the locals live at its suspension point, in reverse declaration order" — nothing about `defer`. `[CTL-7]`: "`defer:` registers a block to run when the enclosing block exits"; `[CTL-8]`: "On every exit from a block, its `defer` blocks run first" — dropping a frame is not an exit of its block in any rule, and `[CTL-7]`'s uses "at every exit" (`E3040`, `E3060`) do not say whether the drop is one. `[PHIL-14]` gives Python's meaning where it costs nothing, and Python runs `finally` on `close()`.
findings.proposed_text:
* `[CORO-7]` *(changed)* Dropping a suspended generator is an exit of every block its suspension point lies in: it runs the `defer` blocks registered in those blocks, last registered first, innermost block first, as `[CTL-8]` runs them at a block's exit, and then drops exactly the locals live at the suspension point, in reverse declaration order. A `defer` block's uses are uses at that exit too (`[CTL-7]`), so a view it uses is not ended before the `yield` (`E3060`). A `defer` block in a `gen fn` cannot `yield` (`E2160`, as it cannot `return`), and the effects of dropping a suspended frame include those of the `defer` blocks it runs (`[EFF-1]`).
* `[CTL-7]` add: "The drop of a suspended generator frame is an exit of the blocks its `yield` lies in (`[CORO-7]`)."
findings.codes: E2160 (yield inside a defer block of a gen fn), E3060

findings.title: Extends O1: a loop of owners closed inside a library's store of a function value or `dyn I` value is seen by neither package (a leak `[PHIL-10]` promises away)
findings.program:
# package `ui` (a library, compiled first)
pub class Button:
    handler: fn() = fn() => pass

    pub fn on_click(owns f: fn()):
        this.handler = f            # the store; `ui`'s graph of owners has no edge from `fn()` to any type that owns a Button

# the program
from ui import Button

class Panel:
    name: String
    btn: Button = Button()

fn main():
    p = shares mut Panel(name=String("p"))
    q = shares mut p
    p.btn.on_click(owns fn() owns q: println(q.name))   # <-- closes p -> btn -> handler's state -> q -> p; this line is a call, not a store, and the store is in a package already compiled; nothing opens the loop
findings.why: `[WK-5]`: "The compiler builds a graph of owner edges among types ... over the whole program: ... a function value's state, from every function the program can put there"; `[WK-7]`: "A store of an owner ... into a place of an object may close a loop when the stored value's type can reach the holder's type through owner edges; such a line is `E3032` unless ..." — the line that stores is `this.handler = f` in `ui`, whose build sees no program; the program's line is a call, which no rule names as the closing line. `[BLD-14]` item 7 records "the function values the package stores into each place" for the dependant, but no rule reads it for `[WK-6]`. `[BLD-1]`: packages compile separately.
findings.proposed_text: * `[WK-7]` add: "**A store made by a called function counts on the line of the call, in the caller's package.** Each package builds its graph of owners over the types its build sees (its own, its dependencies', and what it puts into a function type or a `dyn I`), and checks every line of its own that may close a loop: a store written in it, and a call whose argument (an owner, a value holding one, a function value whose state owns one) the callee's summary stores into a place reached from another argument of the call, from `this`, or from a module variable (`[BLD-14]` item 7, the stored function values and the places they go). Through a function type or `dyn I` the owner edge is to every type the caller's build puts there. The call is `E3032` unless the loop it closes is proved opened or one of proofs (1) and (2) holds for the argument, with the message naming the callee's store (\"`p.btn.on_click(...)` (line 12) closes a loop of owners (`p` → `btn` → the handler's `q` → `p`) through `on_click`'s store (`ui`, line 6) that nothing opens again before `p` ends; open it before `main` ends: `p.btn.on_click(owns fn() => pass)`, or capture `weakref q`\")." `[WK-5]`: replace "over the whole program" with "over the types each package's build sees, as `[WK-7]` says".

findings.title: Extends O1: a library's own line whose verdict rests on what the program puts in a function value or behind a `dyn` method is re-checked by nobody
findings.program:
# package `bus` (a library, compiled first)
pub class Bus:
    log: Array[String] = []
    handlers: Array[fn(StrView)] = []

    pub fn on(owns f: fn(StrView)):
        this.handlers.push(owns f)

    pub fn flush():
        for line in this.log:          # a walk of this.log
            for h in this.handlers:
                h(line)                # changes what every function the program puts in `handlers` changes ([EFF-2]): nothing, when `bus` is built

# the program
from bus import Bus

fn main():
    b = shares mut Bus()
    b2 = shares mut b
    b.on(owns fn(s) owns b2: b2.log.push(owns String(s)))   # <-- now `flush`'s `h(line)` pushes to the list `flush` walks (E3020 by [BRW-18]) in a body no build checks again; [CLO-17]'s E3022 does not apply (the function reshapes `log`, not the place `handlers` that holds it)
    b.flush()
findings.why: `[BCK-8]`: "Summaries are the least fixed point over the whole program's call graph ... across a package's edge each is recorded in the package's interface file"; `[EFF-4]`: "A change to any of them is reported as an interface change and re-checks every caller" — a program that puts a function into a library's place changes the library's summary from below, and the library's `flush` is not a caller of anything the program wrote; `[BLD-14]` item 7 records the stored functions "which a program using the package counts wherever such a value is called" — at the program's calls, not at the library's own walk. `[CLO-17]` refuses only a store into "a place that a real variable it changes owns ... nor in a place that its body may reshape or end through a name it captured".
findings.proposed_text: * `[BCK-8]` add: "**Which build checks a line.** A line whose verdict rests on what the whole program puts in a place (a call through a function value, an interface, a `dyn` or `virtual` method, a foreign call, a `drop` of a `dyn` value) is checked by its own package with what that build sees, and checked again, with the same rules, by every package that puts a new function, implementation or callback there (`[BLD-14]` item 7, the interface file naming each such line with the places it calls through): a refusal is reported in that package at the line that puts it, naming the other package's line and the chain of calls (`E3020`, `E3021`, `E3022`, `E3031`, `E7018` as the case decides): \"`b.on(...)` (line 7) stores a function that pushes to `b2.log`, and `Bus.flush` (`bus`, line 10) walks `this.log` while it runs the handlers (its line 12); push to a list of your own in the handler and move it into the log after `flush`\". A line checked this way in no build is a defect of the build (`[PHIL-12]`)." `[EFF-4]`: after "re-checks every caller" add "and every line checked against that place (`[BCK-8]`)".
findings.codes: E3020, E3021, E3022, E3031, E7018 at the storing line (shapes B2, B3, B1, B16)

findings.title: Extends O1: a contract verdict through a `dyn` or `virtual` call depends on implementations another package adds later
findings.program:
# package `shapes` (a library)
pub interface Shape:
    fn area() -> float

@noalloc
pub fn total(xs: Array[owns dyn Shape]) -> float:
    t = 0.0
    for s in xs:
        t += s.area()          # [EFF-2]: the effects of every implementation the program has; `shapes` sees none that allocates
    return t

# the program
from shapes import Shape, total

static mut LOG: Array[String] = []

struct Logged:
    r: float

extend Logged implements Shape:
    fn area() -> float:
        LOG.push(owns String("area"))    # <-- Alloc: `total` now reaches an allocation under `@noalloc`; which package reports E4001, at which line, and `shapes` is already built
        return 3.14 * this.r * this.r

fn main():
    println(total([owns Logged(r=1.0)]))
findings.why: `[EFF-2]`: "For an interface, `dyn` or `virtual` method, it is every implementation and override the program has"; `[EFF-6]`: "A contract is checked over the whole reachable call graph — callees, drop glue, ... interface implementations reached statically"; `[EFF-5]`: "a violation is the listed error" — the verdict is per program, the function is compiled per package (`[BLD-1]`), and no rule names the package or the line that reports it. `[EFF-2]` already has the per-implementation form: "An interface method may declare contracts; its implementations MUST satisfy them (`E4010`)".
findings.proposed_text: * `[EFF-6]` add: "**A contract through an interface.** Inside a function that carries a contract, a call through a `dyn I` value, through a `virtual` method of a `pub` `open` or `abstract` class, or through a type parameter's bound, counts the implementations the function's own package sees. Since another package may add one, such a call is admitted under the contract only when the interface's method or the `virtual` method declares that contract itself (`[EFF-2]`), which holds every implementation to it where it is written (`E4010`); a generic bounded by the interface is checked per instance, by the package that makes the instance. Otherwise the call is the contract's error (`E4001`, `E4002`, ...) at the call, whose help gives both lines: \"`total` is `@noalloc`, and `s.area()` runs whichever `area` the program gives a `Shape`; hold every `Shape` to it: write `@noalloc` above `fn area() -> float` in `interface Shape`, or take the shape as a type parameter: `[S: needs Shape]` above `fn total(xs: Array[S])`\"." `[DET-3]`: the same sentence for `@deterministic` and `E4070`.
findings.codes: E4001–E4042, E4070 at the call; E4010 at each implementation

findings.title: "A function from a variable given to a standard-library function is lent": the same first line in the program's own package reads the opposite way
findings.program:
[F: needs fn(int)]
fn apply(owns f: F):          # the first line `for_each` has: `fn for_each(owns f: F) owns this`
    f(5)

fn main():
    h = fn(x: int): println(x)
    [1, 2].iter().for_each(h)   # a standard-library function: `h` is lent, `h` stays the caller's (verdict 150)
    apply(h)                    # <-- the program's own function with the same first line: lent, or E3028 "say so at the call: `apply(owns h)`", after which `h(7)` is E3040?
    h(7)
findings.why: `[FN-2a]`: "A function from a variable given to a standard-library function that takes one is lent and takes no word: after `xs.iter().for_each(h)`, `h` is the caller's still"; `[STD-19]`: "A function from a variable is lent to the call and takes no word" — both name the standard library, and `[OWN-9]`: "An argument for an `owns` parameter says `owns` at the call" for everyone else. `[PHIL-1]`: "Two syntactically identical declarations in the same context have identical storage, lifetime and synchronisation behaviour"; `[PHIL-16]`: the words say what the code does. A compiler must special-case `std` by name, which `[TYP-43]` forbids for types ("recognised by the module that declares them, never by their names") and no rule allows for functions.
findings.proposed_text: * `[FN-2a]` replace "A function from a variable given to a standard-library function that takes one is lent and takes no word: after `xs.iter().for_each(h)`, `h` is the caller's still (`[STD-19]`)." with: "A function from a variable given to a parameter whose type is a type parameter bounded by a function type (`owns f: F` under `[F: needs fn(int)]`, `[CLO-14]`), in any package, is lent for the call and takes no word: `F` names that very function, the callee runs it and owns nothing of it, so after `xs.iter().for_each(h)` and after `apply(h)` alike `h` is the caller's still, and a value the call gives back that keeps it (an iterator adapter, `[STD-19]`) is a value holding a view of `h`, which lives no longer than `h` (`[LT-45]`). `owns h` before such an argument is `E0109` (\"`apply` runs `h` and keeps nothing of it; remove `owns`: `apply(h)`\"); a function written in the call is given with `owns` (verdict 158). A parameter of a callable type (`owns f: fn(int)`) keeps what it is given, and takes `owns` as any `owns` parameter does." `[STD-19]`: "A function from a variable is lent to the call and takes no word, as to any function that takes it as a type parameter (`[FN-2a]`)".
findings.codes: E0109 (owns before a lent function), E3028 unchanged for callable-typed parameters
findings.touches_owner_verdict: 150 (generalised from standard-library functions to every function with that first line; the verdict's own programs keep their meaning)

findings.title: A `static` whose value owns heap memory behind a `Mutex`: `[STA-3]` puts it in the image, `[CT-5]` builds it on first access
findings.program:
from std.sync import Mutex

static LOG: Mutex[Array[String]] = Mutex([String("start")])   # <-- [STA-3]: evaluable at compile time, not `static mut`: "placed in the image with no initialisation code"; [CT-5]: "the initialiser runs at run time on first access"

fn main():
    with g = LOG.lock():
        g.push(owns String("more"))     # grows a buffer that one reading placed in read-only memory
findings.why: `[STA-3]`: "A static whose initialiser can be evaluated at compile time is placed in the image with no initialisation code, except a `static mut` whose value owns heap memory, which its functions may grow or free: that value is built on first access" — the exception names `static mut` only. `[CT-5]`: "in a `static mut`, and in any other `static` whose memory a safe operation may write (`static LOG: Mutex[Array[String]] = Mutex([])`), the initialiser runs at run time on first access (`[STA-3]`)" — cites `[STA-3]` for what `[STA-3]` does not say. A compiler following `[STA-3]` lets `push` realloc constant data.
findings.proposed_text: * `[STA-3]` replace "except a `static mut` whose value owns heap memory, which its functions may grow or free: that value is built on first access, never in read-only memory (`[CT-5]`)" with: "except a value that owns heap memory (an `Array`, `String`, `Map`, `Set`, an `owns T`, a class object) in a `static mut`, or in a `static` whose type gives some name a way to change the value (a `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Cell`, `Atomic`, `Once` or `guarded by` field on the path to it, `[CT-5]`): that value is built on first access, never in read-only memory, so that nothing grows, changes or frees constant data."
findings.milestone: M15 (the evaluator and image placement); M9 for the Mutex path

findings.title: A view (`StrView`, `Span[T]`) in an exported signature: neither admitted nor refused, with a C ABI stated for one and a validation rule against the other
findings.program:
# SAFETY: the host defines no other symbol named `game_log`
@unsafe(export("game_log"))
pub extern "C" fn log_line(s: StrView, xs: Span[i32]) -> i32:   # <-- [FFI-31b] lists neither `StrView` nor `Span` in what MUST NOT nor in what may cross; [TXT-6] gives `StrView` the shape `{ptr, len}`; [TXT-2] says nothing becomes a `StrView` without validation
    println(s, xs.len())
    return 0
findings.why: `[FFI-31b]`: "class objects, `owns T`, ... MUST NOT appear in an exported signature ... `@layout(c)` values, scalars, opaque handles, `CStrView` and `extern \"C\" fn` may" — views are in neither list; `[TXT-6]`: "Across the C ABI a `StrView` is `{const uint8_t *ptr; size_t len}`"; `[TXT-2]`: "Nothing becomes a `StrView` without validation ... An importer or binding that would hand foreign bytes to a `StrView` without validation is `E5063`"; `[BLD-FFI-5]`: the C++ header takes `std::span` "where the C header takes pointer-and-length pairs", which only an exported view would produce. Under `[PHIL-12]` the export is `E0901`, and `[TXT-6]` then describes nothing.
findings.proposed_text: * `[FFI-31b]` add: "A `Span[T]` or `MutSpan[T]` whose `T` is a scalar or a `@layout(c)` value type may appear in an exported signature, and crosses as a pointer and a count (`[TXT-6]`'s shape; `MutSpan` under `ref mut`, `[FN-1a]`): that the count is right and the memory lives for the call is C's side of the export's contract, an asserted fact `ember tcb` lists (`[TCB-1]`). A `StrView` may not: C would hand bytes to it unvalidated (`E5063`: \"`s` would be text C never validated; take `s: Span[u8]` and write `s.to_str()?` for the `StrView`, `[TXT-2]`\"), and neither may a `ref T`, a `ref mut T`, a `MutSpan` of any other `T`, or a view type (`E5015`), whose lifetime nothing states." `[TXT-6]`: add "(a `StrView` crosses only as an import's counted contract makes one, `[FFI-10]`, or as the `Span[u8]` an export takes)".

findings.title: Costs the rules introduce with no row in §X.4: the hidden drop flag, a static's first-access test, the hand-over's weak-count compare and its move into a new block
findings.why: `[COST-5]`: "A rule that introduces an implicit cost MUST add a row to this table"; `[PHIL-15]`: "Every cost the language can insert without the programmer writing it ... has a row in §X.4". `[OWN-3]`: "A value handed over on only some paths is tracked with a hidden drop flag"; `[STA-3]`: "Any other initialiser runs **once**, on first access ... the first access blocks until it completes"; `[THR-2]`: "At the hand-over the program reads the object's weak count, one compare. ... its contents move to a new block for the other thread" — none has a row, and `[PHIL-2]`'s list of allocating forms ("No heap allocation happens that the source does not show") lacks the hand-over's new block.
findings.proposed_text: * `[COST-3]` add three rows: "| A value handed over on some paths only | guaranteed present | one hidden drop flag in the frame: a store at the hand-over and one test where the owner would end (`[OWN-3]`); none where every path hands it over or none does |"; "| First access of a `static` built on first access (`[STA-3]`) | guaranteed present | one test of its once-flag per access, and the initialiser once; none for a static placed in the image |"; "| A one-owner object handed to another thread (`[THR-2]`) | guaranteed present | one compare of its weak count, and one for each object it owns whose class a `weakref` may name; with a link, one allocation and a move of its contents into a new block (`Alloc`, listed by `ember inspect --alloc`) |". `[PHIL-2]`: add to the allocating forms "a one-owner object handed to another thread while a `weakref` link names it (`[THR-2]`)". `[EFF-1]`: a read of a static built on first access carries its initialiser's effects, `Block` included.
findings.milestone: text only (rows); M9 for the hand-over's Alloc

findings.title: "unless the compiler already knows the ranges are disjoint" names no proof, so an `@no_alias_checks` verdict may differ between implementations
findings.why: `[DSJ-5]`: "Both forms record a `RuntimeCheck(Aliasing)` site ... unless the compiler already knows the ranges are disjoint, in which case no comparison is emitted"; `[EFF-15]`: "The proofs that count are exactly those this document specifies — `[OPT-2]`, `[RNG-4]`, `[SIMD-7]` and the parent-link proof of Part VIII ... a verdict is computed as if every one of them were applied"; `[EFF-12]`: `E4030` where the compare survives. What "already knows" means decides `E4030`.
findings.proposed_text: * `[DSJ-5]` replace "unless the compiler already knows the ranges are disjoint, in which case no comparison is emitted" with "unless the two names are proved apart when compiling by `[BRW-5]`'s and `[SIMD-3]`'s structural facts (two constant indices that differ, `j` from `i + 1..`, the line inside `if i != j:`, the two halves of one `split_at`, two chunks of one `chunks_mut`, two distinct `SoA` columns), in which case no comparison is emitted and no `RuntimeCheck(Aliasing)` is recorded; these are the only facts that remove it, and `[EFF-15]` counts them among the proofs that decide a verdict." `[EFF-15]`: add `[DSJ-5]`'s structural facts to the list.

findings.title: An arithmetic operation on constants whose result does not fit: refused when compiling or a panic while running
findings.why: `[TYP-8]`: "An arithmetic operation ... whose mathematical result does not fit its type panics"; `[LEX-16]`: "A value that does not fit the resulting type is `E2010`" (a literal); `[TYP-30]`: "a negative exponent is `E2151` when it is a constant and a panic when it is not" — the constant case is decided for the sign and not for the overflow; `[TYP-41]` rule 1 decides it only for a `const` argument (`E6004`). One compiler folds and refuses, another emits the panic: the set of accepted programs differs.
findings.proposed_text: * `[TYP-8]` add: "An operation whose operands are numbers the compiler knows (numbers written as numbers, `const` items, and arithmetic on them, `[STD-19]`) is computed when compiling under the policy of its place: under `panic` a result that does not fit, a zero divisor or an exponent below zero is refused, `E2010` (\"`2 ** 70` does not fit `int`; compute it in a wider type, `2u128 ** 70`, or let it wrap: `2.wrapping_pow(70)`\"), as a literal that does not fit is (`[LEX-16]`); under `wrap` or `saturate` the result is the policy's. A result that fits is the operation's, and no check runs for it (`[RNG-4]`)." Registry `E2010`: "a number written in the program, a literal or an operation on known numbers, does not fit its type".
findings.codes: E2010 (widened to constant arithmetic), E2151 unchanged
findings.milestone: text only (today's type checker folds constants; no milestone owns it)

    hi: int = lo + 1                  # <-- an earlier field in a default: in scope? [STR-2]: "any expression"

findings.title: A name for a part of a list element (`ref mut enemies[0].hp`): a position found again, or an address a `push` ends
findings.program:
struct Enemy:
    hp: int

fn main():
    enemies = [Enemy(hp=1), Enemy(hp=2)]
    h = ref mut enemies[0].hp        # <-- made by indexing and then a field: [BRW-16] names "a list element made by indexing"; [BRW-17] takes "every other view"
    enemies.push(owns Enemy(hp=3))   # moves the buffer: a position survives, an address is ended
    h += 1                           # E3060 under [BRW-17]; accepted under a reading of [BRW-16]
findings.why: `[BRW-16]`: "A name for a list element made by indexing (`boss = enemies[0]`, `boss = ref mut enemies[0]`...) ... is a position: the index is read once ... and the element is found again at each use"; `[BRW-17]`: "Every other view (... a view into a value's own contents ...) ends at any change that may reshape what it points into"; `[BCK-1]` repeats both. A part of an element is "made by indexing" and a field access; the text's "every other" makes it an address, but nothing says it, and the index-plus-offset re-find is as cheap and as safe.
findings.proposed_text: * `[BRW-16]` add: "A name for a part of such an element (`h = ref mut enemies[0].hp`, `n = enemies[i].name`), reached by fields alone from the element, is a position too: the index is kept with it and the part is found again at each use through the list's current buffer. A view that goes on from the part through a call, a link or into a value's own contents (`enemies[0].name.trim()`) is an address (`[BRW-17]`)." `[BCK-1]`: the same words after "found again at each use".

findings.title: "the tasks of scopes it opens": a scope opened inside a scoped task of the main thread
findings.program:
import std.thread

static mut HITS: int = 0

fn inner_work():
    with inner = thread.scope():      # a scope opened by a task, not by the main thread's own frame
        inner.spawn(owns fn(): HITS += 1)    # <-- [THR-20]: reached "by the main thread and the tasks of scopes it opens": is a task of a scope a task opened one?

fn main():
    with outer = thread.scope():
        outer.spawn(owns fn(): inner_work())
    println(HITS)
findings.why: `[THR-20]`: "A `static mut` (`[STA-1]`) is reached only by the main thread and the tasks of scopes it opens"; `[STA-1]`: "reached only by the main thread and its scoped tasks" — a scope opened by a task is opened by the task's thread, and the two sentences can be read as one level deep or any depth. The reduction `HITS += 1` is safe at any depth (`[THR-21]`, the join orders it), so the deeper reading costs nothing.
findings.proposed_text: * `[THR-20]` replace "reached only by the main thread and the tasks of scopes it opens" with "reached only by the main thread and the tasks of the scopes opened on it, at any depth: a scope opened inside such a task is on the main thread's stack of scopes, and its tasks are checked by `[THR-11]` against every task of every open scope of that stack and against the main thread; a `thread.spawn` thread, a job submitted outside a scope and the scopes they open are not". `[STA-1]`: "and the tasks of its scopes, at any depth (`[THR-20]`)".

verdicts.reason: `[CLO-10]`: "what it captured with a word, in one block of its own made with the value (it carries `Alloc` ...), except that a state of one word or less may be kept in the state word itself, with no block" — "may" is a permission to the implementation, while `[PHIL-2]` speaks of "a function value whose state exceeds its inline capacity (`[CLO-10]`)" as if the capacity were fixed; nothing fixes it, so whether `fn() owns n: n += 1` carries `Alloc` (`E4001` under `@noalloc`, `[EFF-5]`) differs between implementations, against `[PHIL-13]` and `[EFF-15]`. On the copy-out: `[CLO-10]` "A call through a list element or a field copies the two words out before the arguments are given and keeps no pointer into the list or field" and `[BRW-1]` "uses the name only to copy the function's two words out ... so the call's arguments may reach the place it names" describe a call made on a copy; `[CLO-18]` says only the effect ("is a change of the place that holds it") and no sentence writes the two words back, which with an inline one-word state loses `calls += 1`. A write-back cannot be the answer either: `[BRW-1]` lets the call's arguments reshape the holder's place meanwhile. The three goals favour the reader's shape: a state the body may write lives in a block (so a copied-out pointer still reaches it), and `[CLO-18]`'s own words "a state block is not counted (`[CLO-10]`)" already assume a self-changing function has one.
verdicts.better_fix: * `[CLO-10]` replace "except that a state of one word or less may be kept in the state word itself, with no block" with: "except that a state of one word or less that the function's body never writes is kept in the state word itself, with no block and no `Alloc`: a `copy of` of a `Copy` value it only reads, or an owner or a link it only reads through. A body writes its state when, in the body or in a function it calls with the captured name, the name is assigned or augmented, named `ref mut`, given to a `ref mut` or `owns` parameter, handed over, or has a method called on it that changes it, worked out as `[EFF-24]` works out what a function changes; such a state lives in a block of its own, so that a call through a copy of the two words (a list element, a field, `[BRW-1]`) changes the state the holder keeps. Which of the two a function value has is decided from its captures and its body alone, the same in every implementation (`[PHIL-13]`); its `Alloc` is at the line that makes the function value, which `ember inspect --alloc` lists, and `E4001` there names it: \"`counter` is `@noalloc`, and the function made on line 4 keeps `n`, which it changes (`n += 1`), in a block of its own; keep the count in the caller's variable instead: `fn counter(ref mut n: int)`\"." Add to `[CLO-18]`: "The two words copied out before the call (`[CLO-10]`) point at the state the holder keeps, never at a copy of it: a function value that changes its own state has a block, so the change is the holder's after the call." `[PHIL-2]`: replace "whose state exceeds its inline capacity" with "whose state has a block (`[CLO-10]`: more than one word, or a word its body writes)".

verdicts.reason: `[RC-1]`: "`shares x`, `shares mut x` and `thread_shared x` are written before a new value, a local of this function that owns its value (...) or a name that is already such an owner" — "such an owner" covers the three kinds together, and `[OWN-13]`'s "each written only before a new value, a local or an owner (`[RC-1]`, `E2122`)" names no kind either; `[THR-1]` refuses only the reverse ("on a value made otherwise it is `E7017`"). So `q = shares p` for `p: thread_shared Player` is admitted and `q`'s type is the shared type of its word, `shares Player`. Two promises then break: `[THR-2]` "A `shares` or `shares mut` owner counts its owners with plain adds" on a value whose header `[RC-4]` keeps as "home ... read and written only by that thread, with plain instructions" and an atomic away count — on `look`'s thread a plain add races with the making thread's; and `q = shares mut p` gives an owner that `[RC-7]` lets change the value directly ("A value made shared is changed by its owners that may change it: an owner made with `shares mut`"), which `[THR-1]`'s first rule forbids for a `thread_shared` value only by its word, which `q` no longer carries. No sentence says which count or instruction such an owner uses, so at best `E0901`, at worst a race. The proposed text is general and keeps the three goals; `E7017` widened to "an owner word that does not match how the value was made" fits its registry row.

The text decides the drop case, though not in `[CORO-7]`: `[EFF-1]` says "dropping a suspended one [carries the effects of] those of the drops it performs (ODR-057)", which is consistent only with `defer` blocks not running (their effects would otherwise be in the set), and `[CORO-7]` "drops exactly the locals live at its suspension point" names nothing else. `[PHIL-14]` does not reach it: `defer` is not a Python spelling, and `[PAN-1]` already keeps `defer` blocks from running on a panic. What is real: `[CORO-7]` never names `defer`, so an implementer finds the answer only through `[EFF-1]`'s effect sentence; and a `yield` written inside a `defer` block of a `gen fn` is refused by no rule (`[CTL-7]` lists `return`, `break`, `continue` for `E2160`; `[CORO-2]` refuses `yield` only outside a `gen fn`), and what a suspension in the middle of a block's exit means is said nowhere (`E0901` by `[PHIL-12]`).

A value whose clean-up must run however the generator ends is a value with a `drop`, which the frame's drop ends, not a `defer` block. A `yield` inside a `defer` block is `E2160` ("a `defer` block runs while its block exits, and `yield` would suspend the generator in the middle of that exit; yield before the block exits, or move the `defer` line below the `yield`"), as `return`, `break` and `continue` are. (If the owner prefers Python's `finally`-on-close instead, the reader's text is the shape to write, and `[EFF-1]`'s sentence changes with it; either choice must be written, and this one costs nothing and changes no effect set.)
